Manually fit and pool Cox proportional hazards model results from multiple imputed datasets

Source: R/cox_pooling.R
cox_pooling.Rd

This function manually fits and pools results from Cox proportional hazards models using a list of imputed datasets. It leverages the mice::as.mira and mice::pool functions to ensure proper pooling of results across multiple imputations using Rubin's rules.

Usage

cox_pooling(
  x,
  surv_formula = stats::as.formula(survival::Surv(fu_itt_months, death_itt) ~ treat),
  ...
)

Arguments

x

The imputed datasets to analyze. One of:

  • a list of data frames (one per imputed dataset), e.g., the output of raking_weights or of MatchThem::complete(..., action = "all")

  • a weighted (wimids) or matched (mimids) object created with MatchThem

  • an imputed (mids) object created with mice

See the section "Input types and default model arguments" for how each input is handled.

surv_formula

A formula for the Cox proportional hazards model (default is Surv(fu_itt_months, death_itt) ~ treat).

...

Additional arguments passed on to the per-dataset model call (survfit2 for km_pooling(), coxph for cox_pooling()). They are used in addition to, and take precedence over, the default arguments of the input type (see the section "Input types and default model arguments"). Only formula and data are set internally and cannot be supplied here. Column names are written without quotes and are looked up in each dataset, e.g. weights = w or id = patientid.

Value

A data frame containing the pooled results, including hazard ratios, confidence intervals, and p-values.

Details

The function takes the imputed datasets (x) as a list of data frames, or as a mimids, wimids or mids object (see the sections "Input types and default model arguments" and "Precedence of arguments in ..." below), as well as a formula for the Cox proportional hazards model. Weights and clusters of lists of data frames are specified explicitly via ..., e.g., weights = weights for weighted data and weights = weights, cluster = subclass for matched data. A list is particularly useful when working with imputed datasets that are not in the form of mimids or wimids objects, such as when intermediate steps like raking weights (via raking_weights) are applied. Arguments of the coxph call can be supplied via ..., e.g., ties = "breslow".

Breaking change in 0.4.0: previously, a list of data frames had to contain a column named weights, which was used automatically, as was a column named subclass (cluster membership of matched datasets). Weights and clusters are no longer applied automatically to lists, in line with km_pooling. Update calls such as cox_pooling(x, surv_formula) to cox_pooling(x, surv_formula, weights = weights) (weighted data) or cox_pooling(x, surv_formula, weights = weights, cluster = subclass) (matched data). Calls that are not updated fit an unweighted model and raise a warning that names the unused columns. mimids and wimids objects are not affected.

The function follows these steps:

  1. Fit a Cox proportional hazards model to each imputed dataset, using the weights and cluster (if any) of the input type or specified via ....

  2. Convert the list of fitted models into a mira object using mice::as.mira.

  3. Pool the results using mice::pool, which applies Rubin's rules for combining estimates and variances across imputations.

  4. Format the pooled results, including exponentiating the hazard ratios and calculating confidence intervals.

Input types and default model arguments

The datasets are first brought into the form of a list of data frames. Depending on the type of x, default model arguments are set:

Input xHow the datasets are obtainedweightscluster
wimidsMatchThem::complete(x, action = "all", all = FALSE, include = FALSE)weightsnone
mimidssame as wimidsweightssubclass
midsmice::complete(x, action = "all", include = FALSE)none (unweighted)none
list of data framesused as suppliednonenone

Lists of data frames are never interpreted automatically. A list can come from many sources (weighting, matching, raking, your own code) so the function cannot know which columns are meant as weights or clusters. You state this explicitly through ..., for example:

  • weighted data: weights = weights

  • matched data: weights = weights, cluster = subclass

  • weights stored in a column with another name: weights = w

If the datasets contain a column named weights or subclass that is not used because no weights or cluster (or id) argument was specified, a warning is raised that names the argument to add. Specify weights = NULL or cluster = NULL to confirm that the column should deliberately be ignored.

Important: when you build the list from a mimids or wimids object yourself, use MatchThem::complete(x, action = "all", all = FALSE, include = FALSE). With all = TRUE, unmatched patients and patients with zero weight are included in the models.

Precedence of arguments in ...

Default arguments of the input type are applied first, then the arguments you supply via .... If both contain the same argument, your argument wins. For example, for a mimids object cluster = NULL fits the model without clustering on the matched sets and cluster = pair_id clusters on another column. formula and data are the only reserved arguments.

robust is set automatically: unless you specify it, robust = TRUE is used whenever weights, a cluster or an id are part of the model (the model-based variance is not valid in these cases), otherwise the default of the model function is kept. An explicitly supplied robust always takes precedence.

Transparency

Every call prints a message that lists how the datasets were obtained and exactly which arguments were used for the models, including where each argument comes from (default for the input type, derived, or specified by you). Use suppressMessages() to silence it.

See also

km_pooling, raking_weights, coxph, pool, as.mira, matchthem, weightthem

Examples

library(encore.analytics)
library(mice)
#> 
#> Attaching package: ‘mice’
#> The following object is masked from ‘package:stats’:
#> 
#>     filter
#> The following objects are masked from ‘package:base’:
#> 
#>     cbind, rbind
library(MatchThem)
#> 
#> Attaching package: ‘MatchThem’
#> The following objects are masked from ‘package:mice’:
#> 
#>     cbind, pool
#> The following object is masked from ‘package:base’:
#> 
#>     cbind

# Simulate a cohort with 500 patients and 20% missing data
data <- simulate_data(
  n = 500,
  imposeNA = TRUE,
  propNA = 0.2
)

# Impute the data
set.seed(42)
mids <- mice(data, m = 5, print = FALSE)
#> Warning: Number of logged events: 765

# Fit a propensity score model
fit <- as.formula(treat ~ dem_age_index_cont + dem_sex_cont + c_smoking_history)

# Weight patients within each imputed dataset
wimids <- weightthem(
  formula = fit,
  datasets = mids,
  approach = "within",
  method = "glm",
  estimand = "ATO"
)
#> Estimating weights     | dataset: #1
#>  #2
#>  #3
#>  #4
#>  #5
#> 

# Define a survival model formula
cox_fit <- as.formula(survival::Surv(fu_itt_months, death_itt) ~ treat)

# 1) Weighted (wimids) or matched (mimids) object:
# weights (and clusters) are set automatically
cox_pooling(wimids, surv_formula = cox_fit)
#> ℹ Input: <wimids>: weighted datasets extracted with MatchThem::complete(action
#>   = "all", all = FALSE, include = FALSE) (m = 5)
#> ℹ Fitting Cox proportional hazards model with survival::coxph() in each
#>   dataset:
#>   formula: survival::Surv(fu_itt_months, death_itt) ~ treat
#>   weights = weights (default for the input type)
#>   robust = TRUE (derived: weights, cluster or id are used)
#>    term  estimate  std.error statistic     p.value  conf.low conf.high
#> 1 treat 0.7297697 0.08792742 -3.582799 0.000374082 0.6139819 0.8673933
#>              b       df dfcom       fmi      lambda m         riv        ubar
#> 1 4.570604e-05 487.4987   496 0.0111428 0.007094245 5 0.007144933 0.007676384

# 2) List of data frames: weights are specified explicitly via `...`
# (all = FALSE excludes observations with zero weight)
wimids_list <- MatchThem::complete(wimids, action = "all", all = FALSE, include = FALSE)
cox_pooling(wimids_list, surv_formula = cox_fit, weights = weights)
#> ℹ Input: list of data frames supplied by the user; no weights or cluster
#>   applied automatically (m = 5)
#> ℹ Fitting Cox proportional hazards model with survival::coxph() in each
#>   dataset:
#>   formula: survival::Surv(fu_itt_months, death_itt) ~ treat
#>   weights = weights (specified by you)
#>   robust = TRUE (derived: weights, cluster or id are used)
#>    term  estimate  std.error statistic     p.value  conf.low conf.high
#> 1 treat 0.7297697 0.08792742 -3.582799 0.000374082 0.6139819 0.8673933
#>              b       df dfcom       fmi      lambda m         riv        ubar
#> 1 4.570604e-05 487.4987   496 0.0111428 0.007094245 5 0.007144933 0.007676384

# for matched datasets, additionally specify the matched sets as clusters:
# cox_pooling(matched_list, surv_formula = cox_fit, weights = weights, cluster = subclass)

# 3) Imputed (mids) object: unweighted Cox model
cox_pooling(mids, surv_formula = cox_fit)
#> ℹ Input: <mids>: imputed datasets extracted with mice::complete(action = "all",
#>   include = FALSE); unweighted (m = 5)
#> ℹ Fitting Cox proportional hazards model with survival::coxph() in each
#>   dataset:
#>   formula: survival::Surv(fu_itt_months, death_itt) ~ treat
#>   no weights, cluster or other arguments used
#>    term  estimate  std.error statistic     p.value  conf.low conf.high b
#> 1 treat 0.7494818 0.09202893 -3.133507 0.001829959 0.6255089 0.8980255 0
#>        df dfcom         fmi lambda m riv        ubar
#> 1 493.962   496 0.004024452      0 5   0 0.008469323

# 4) Pass additional arguments to the underlying coxph() call
cox_pooling(wimids, surv_formula = cox_fit, ties = "breslow")
#> ℹ Input: <wimids>: weighted datasets extracted with MatchThem::complete(action
#>   = "all", all = FALSE, include = FALSE) (m = 5)
#> ℹ Fitting Cox proportional hazards model with survival::coxph() in each
#>   dataset:
#>   formula: survival::Surv(fu_itt_months, death_itt) ~ treat
#>   weights = weights (default for the input type)
#>   ties = "breslow" (specified by you)
#>   robust = TRUE (derived: weights, cluster or id are used)
#>    term  estimate  std.error statistic     p.value  conf.low conf.high
#> 1 treat 0.7297697 0.08792742 -3.582799 0.000374082 0.6139819 0.8673933
#>              b       df dfcom       fmi      lambda m         riv        ubar
